claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using two different RNAi lines (pvf1-i1 and pvf1-i2), as shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The increase in TAG content of muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies is more pronounced when flies are challenged with a mildly high-sugar diet.
claims.source: The increase in TAG content of musts>pvf1-i flies was more pronounced when flies were challenged with a mildly high-sugar diet (15% w/v added sugar to our standard food) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing TAG content on standard food versus high-sugar diet, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Knocking down pvf2 or pvf3 in the adult muscle does not affect total TAG content of the animals.
claims.source: Knocking down either pvf2 or pvf3 in the adult muscle did not affect total TAG content of the animals, further demonstrating that the phenotype is specifically associated with muscle-specific loss of Pvf1 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TAG assays comparing pvf1, pvf2, and pvf3 knockdown, as presented in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies and control flies show comparable incorporation of 14C when fed with 14C-U-Glucose for 24 hrs.
claims.source: When fed with 14C-U-Glucose for 24 hrs, musts>pvf1-i and control flies showed comparable incorporation of 14C in whole fly homogenates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that musts>pvf1-i flies do not eat more than control animals and that the obesity phenotype observed is most likely caused by metabolic defects.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioactive glucose feeding assays, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The obesity phenotype in muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies is most likely caused by metabolic defects rather than increased food intake.
claims.source: When fed with 14C-U-Glucose for 24 hrs, musts>pvf1-i and control flies showed comparable incorporation of 14C in whole fly homogenates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that musts>pvf1-i flies do not eat more than control animals and that the obesity phenotype observed is most likely caused by metabolic defects.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing comparable food intake between experimental and control flies.

claims.claim: Pvf1 protein is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles.
claims.source: Pvf1 is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) where it is stored between the individual myofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D1', D3') and is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D3,3',3').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining with anti-Pvf1 antibody, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Pvf1 protein is stored between individual myofibrils in leg muscles.
claims.source: Pvf1 is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) where it is stored between the individual myofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D1', D3') and is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D3,3',3').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining showing Pvf1 localization, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Pvf1 protein is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs in leg muscles.
claims.source: Pvf1 is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) where it is stored between the individual myofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D1', D3') and is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D3,3',3').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining showing Pvf1 localization, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of pvf1 leads to a strong reduction in Pvf1 protein level in leg muscles.

claims.claim: The indirect flight muscles (IFMs) do not show any staining for Pvf1.

claims.claim: Pvf1 protein is primarily stored in the striated tubular muscles in the fly.
claims.source: Interestingly, the IFMs did not show any staining for Pvf1 indicating that the protein is primarily stored in the striated tubular muscles in the fly.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunostaining data showing Pvf1 presence in tubular muscles but not in IFMs.

claims.claim: Single-nuclei RNA-sequencing was performed on adult fly abdominal cuticles to understand transcriptomes of metabolically active tissues.
claims.source: We took advantage of this tool to understand the transcriptomes of tissue types residing in the adult abdominal cuticle that harbors several metabolically active tissues such as the fat body, abdominal-muscles, and oenocytes, which are functionally analogous to adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and liver, respectively, in higher vertebrates (Droujinine and Perrimon, 2016; Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental approach and references to established knowledge about tissue functions.

claims.claim: A total of 80 adult fly abdominal cuticles were dissected and dissociated for single-nuclei RNA-sequencing.
claims.source: To delineate the patterns of gene expression in each of these tissues, we dissected and dissociated a total of 80 adult fly abdominal cuticles (along with the attached adipose tissue and oenocytes) and subjected the single nuclei to 10X genomics-based (Zheng et al., 2017) single-nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental methodology.

claims.claim: Two independent rounds of sequencing were performed on two biological replicates with 40 animals per replicate.
claims.source: Two independent rounds of sequencing were performed on two biological replicates (with 40 animals per replicate) to obtain a median read depth of 8904 reads per nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: The median read depth obtained from snRNA-seq was 8904 reads per nucleus.
claims.source: Two independent rounds of sequencing were performed on two biological replicates (with 40 animals per replicate) to obtain a median read depth of 8904 reads per nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: SoupX was used to eliminate potential ambient RNA contamination from the snRNA-seq analysis.
claims.source: Because tissue dissociations for the single nuclei preparations are often associated with the risk of ambient RNA contamination, our quality control pipeline included SoupX (Young and Behjati, 2018) to eliminate potential ambient RNA from our analysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the quality control methodology and citation to the SoupX method.

claims.claim: Harmony was used to correct for batch effects in the two replicates of snRNA-seq data.
claims.source: Further, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) that is integrated into Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to correct for batch effects in the two replicates to finally retain 15,280 nuclei with a median of 192 genes per nucleus for downstream analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the data analysis methodology and citations to Harmony and Seurat.

claims.claim: After quality control and batch correction, 15,280 nuclei were retained for downstream analysis.
claims.source: Further, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) that is integrated into Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to correct for batch effects in the two replicates to finally retain 15,280 nuclei with a median of 192 genes per nucleus for downstream analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the data analysis results.

claims.claim: The median number of genes detected per nucleus after quality control was 192.
claims.source: Further, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) that is integrated into Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to correct for batch effects in the two replicates to finally retain 15,280 nuclei with a median of 192 genes per nucleus for downstream analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the data analysis results.

claims.claim: Clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 identified 10 unique clusters.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the clustering analysis results presented in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers.
claims.source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers, as presented in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The adipose tissue cluster was identified based on expression of apolpp marker.
claims.source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers.

claims.claim: The oenocyte cluster was identified based on expression of fasn3 marker.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers.

claims.claim: The muscle cluster was identified based on expression of mhc marker.
claims.source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers.

claims.claim: The snRNA-seq data was validated using GAL4 lines for enriched genes Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko.
claims.source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I.

claims.claim: Pellino (Pli) specifically expresses in adipose tissue.
claims.source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Sallimus (sls) specifically expresses in muscle.
claims.source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: Geko specifically expresses in oenocytes.
claims.source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: Minor clusters (4-10) are believed to be remnant tissues likely pertaining to gut/malpighian tubule based on enrichment of specific genes.
claims.source: With regard to the rest of the minor clusters (4-10), we believe most of them are remnant tissues most likely pertaining to gut/malpighian tubule based on the enrichment of alphaTry, Whe, and Mur18B (Clusters 4–6, respectively; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns in the minor clusters.

claims.claim: Clusters 7-10 are likely to be part of the ejaculatory bulb based on enrichment of male-specific genes.
claims.source: On the other hand, we consider clusters 7–10 likely to be part of the ejaculatory bulb (Eb) as they are enriched in certain male-specific genes such as bond, EbpIII, soti, and Ebp, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-J; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns showing enrichment of male-specific genes.

claims.claim: Increasing the resolution of clustering analysis to 0.4 leads to identification of 15 unique clusters with unique gene expression signatures.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing the resolution of the clustering analysis to 0.4 leads to the identification of 15 unique clusters with unique gene expression signatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis at higher resolution, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Some of the clusters identified at resolution 0.4 may reflect potential heterogeneity within the adult adipose tissue.
claims.source: Some of these clusters may reflect potential heterogeneity within the adult adipose tissue.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the biological meaning of the additional clusters identified at higher resolution.

claims.claim: Pathway enrichment analysis reveals EGFR and PVR RTK signaling pathway is highly enriched in oenocytes.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that EGFR and PVR RTK signaling pathway is highly enriched in the oenocytes (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis results presented in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Expression of Egfr is specifically enriched in the adipose tissue.
claims.source: While the expression of Egfr is specifically enriched in the adipose tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-j), we identify the Pvf1 receptor Pvr to be highly enriched in the oenocytes, albeit a mild enrichment seen in the other clusters (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from snRNA-seq analysis, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-j.

claims.claim: Pvr is highly enriched in oenocytes with mild enrichment in other clusters.
claims.source: While the expression of Egfr is specifically enriched in the adipose tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-j), we identify the Pvf1 receptor Pvr to be highly enriched in the oenocytes, albeit a mild enrichment seen in the other clusters (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from snRNA-seq analysis, as presented in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: PvR is present most prominently on the surface of oenocytes followed by adipose tissue cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the prediction from the snRNA-seq analysis, PvR is present most prominently on the surface of the oenocytes followed by the adipose tissue cells (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2E, which is consistent with the snRNA-seq predictions.

claims.claim: In leg muscles and indirect flight muscles, PvR localizes to the muscle sarcolemma.
claims.source: In the leg muscles and indirect flight muscles, PvR localizes to the muscle sarcolemma (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although the level of the protein on the sarcolemma of the leg muscles is relatively weak (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The level of PvR protein on the sarcolemma of leg muscles is relatively weak.
claims.source: In the leg muscles and indirect flight muscles, PvR localizes to the muscle sarcolemma (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although the level of the protein on the sarcolemma of the leg muscles is relatively weak (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific over-expression of pvrDN leads to obesity phenotypes similar to muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies.
claims.source: Impairing PvR signaling in the adult oenocytes, by over-expressing a dominant negative form of the receptor, pvrDN, (oenots>pvrDN) (Brückner et al., 2004) led to obesity phenotypes similar to musts>Pvf1-i flies (Figure 2F, G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and TAG assays, as presented in Figure 2F and 2G, with citation to the pvrDN construct.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific expression of an RNAi against pvr leads to obesity.
claims.source: Similarly, impairing PvR signaling in the oenocyte by expressing an RNAi against pvr (oenots>pvr-i) also leads to obesity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The obesity phenotype from oenocyte-specific pvrDN expression was also observed in female flies.
claims.source: The obesity phenotype was also observed in oenots>pvrDN female flies, indicating that the phenotype is not caused by loss of PvR signaling in the male accessory glands where the PromE-Gal4 driver is also expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Billeter et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from female flies, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, with citation to the PromE-Gal4 driver expression pattern.

claims.claim: The obesity phenotype in oenocyte-specific pvrDN females is not caused by loss of PvR signaling in male accessory glands.
claims.source: The obesity phenotype was also observed in oenots>pvrDN female flies, indicating that the phenotype is not caused by loss of PvR signaling in the male accessory glands where the PromE-Gal4 driver is also expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Billeter et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing the phenotype in females, with citation to the driver expression pattern.

claims.claim: Over-expressing pvrDN in the adult adipose tissue and muscle does not lead to an obesity phenotype.
claims.source: Surprisingly, over-expressing pvrDN in the adult adipose tissue and muscle did not lead to an obesity phenotype indicating that Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in the oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TAG assays and BODIPY staining, as presented in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in the oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance.
claims.source: Surprisingly, over-expressing pvrDN in the adult adipose tissue and muscle did not lead to an obesity phenotype indicating that Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in the oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing tissue-specific effects of PvR manipulation.

claims.claim: Muscle-derived Pvf1 signals specifically to the oenocytes to regulate lipid content of the adipose tissue and steatosis in the oenocytes.
claims.source: These results suggest that muscle-derived Pvf1 signals specifically to the oenocytes to regulate lipid content of the adipose tissue and steatosis in the oenocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing tissue-specific effects.

claims.claim: Two independent and validated RNAi transgenes against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype observed in oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies.
claims.source: Two independent and validated RNAi transgenes against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype observed in oenots>pvrDN flies, suggesting that PvR signaling in the oenocytes regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism (Figure 3A, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements using two ERK RNAi lines, as presented in Figure 3A and 3C.

claims.claim: PvR signaling in the oenocytes regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism.
claims.source: Two independent and validated RNAi transgenes against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype observed in oenots>pvrDN flies, suggesting that PvR signaling in the oenocytes regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism (Figure 3A, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing no effect of ERK knockdown on lipid accumulation.

claims.claim: Previous studies in Drosophila S2 and Kc cells have shown that PvR can activate the TOR pathway.
claims.source: Previous studies in Drosophila S2 and Kc cells have shown that PvR can also activate the TOR pathway (Sopko et al., 2015; Tran et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in cell culture systems.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific over-expression of tsc1 and tsc2 leads to massive accumulation of neutral lipids in both adipose tissue and oenocytes.
claims.source: Similar to musts>pvf1-i and oenots>pvrDN flies, oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies showed massive accumulation of neutral lipids in both the adipose tissue and the oenocytes (Figure 3B, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific knockdown of Pi3K92E leads to steatosis phenotypes.
claims.source: Oenocyte-specific loss of either Pi3K92E and the regulatory subunit Pi3K21B led to steatosis phenotypes (Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific knockdown of Pi3K21B leads to steatosis phenotypes.
claims.source: Oenocyte-specific loss of either Pi3K92E and the regulatory subunit Pi3K21B led to steatosis phenotypes (Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific loss of akt1 leads to steatosis phenotypes.
claims.source: Additionally, oenocyte-specific loss of akt1 also led to steatosis phenotypes indicating that the Pi3K-Akt1 pathway in the oenocytes regulates lipid homeostasis (Figure 3D, E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: The Pi3K-Akt1 pathway in the oenocytes regulates lipid homeostasis.
claims.source: Additionally, oenocyte-specific loss of akt1 also led to steatosis phenotypes indicating that the Pi3K-Akt1 pathway in the oenocytes regulates lipid homeostasis (Figure 3D, E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of Pi3K and Akt1 manipulation on lipid accumulation.

claims.claim: Pi3K/Akt1/TOR signaling in the oenocyte protects against obesity.
claims.source: Taken together, these results reveal that Pi3K/Akt1/TOR signaling in the oenocyte protects against obesity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing effects of pathway components on obesity.

claims.claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies show a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in oenocytes compared to controls.
claims.source: Both musts>pvf1-i flies and oenots>pvrDN flies showed a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in the oenocytes compared to Gal4 alone controls (Figure 4A, B, C), indicating that muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from p4EBP immunostaining, as presented in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific pvrDN over-expression flies show a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in oenocytes compared to controls.
claims.source: Both musts>pvf1-i flies and oenots>pvrDN flies showed a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in the oenocytes compared to Gal4 alone controls (Figure 4A, B, C), indicating that muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from p4EBP immunostaining, as presented in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: Muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
claims.source: Both musts>pvf1-i flies and oenots>pvrDN flies showed a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in the oenocytes compared to Gal4 alone controls (Figure 4A, B, C), indicating that muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing reduced p4EBP levels (a TOR target) upon Pvf/PvR pathway disruption.

claims.claim: The extent of p4EBP down-regulation in muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies is similar to oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies.
claims.source: Consistently, the extent of p4EBP down-regulation is similar to what is observed in oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies that were used as a positive control for the assay (Figure 4B, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing p4EBP levels across different genotypes, as presented in Figure 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific loss of insulin receptor signaling does not affect p4EBP levels.
claims.source: Interestingly, oenocyte-specific loss of insulin receptor signaling (oenots>inrDN) failed to affect p4EBP levels (Figure 4B , C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from p4EBP immunostaining, as presented in Figure 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific tsc2 knockdown strongly suppresses the obesity phenotype induced by oenocyte-specific pvrDN expression.
claims.source: tsc2 knockdown strongly suppressed the obesity phenotype induced by oenocyte-specific expression of pvrDN (Figure 4D, E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific co-expression of constitutively active rheb (rhebAV4) completely rescues the obesity phenotype observed in oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies.
claims.source: Oenocyte-specific co-expression of rhebAV4 completely rescued the obesity phenotype observed in oenots>pvrDN flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: TOR signaling functions downstream of PvR in the oenocyte to negatively regulate lipid deposits.
claims.source: Altogether, these observations suggest that TOR signaling functions downstream of PvR in the oenocyte to negatively regulate lipid deposits.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including p4EBP measurements and genetic rescue experiments.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, insulin/Pi3K/Akt signaling can activate the TOR pathway, similar to vertebrates.
claims.source: Similar to vertebrates, the Drosophila TOR pathway can be activated by insulin/Pi3K/Akt signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about TOR pathway regulation in Drosophila and vertebrates.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific over-expression of inrDN does not show any increase in lipid accumulation in adipose tissue or oenocytes compared to control flies.
claims.source: oenots>inrDN flies did not show any increase in accumulation of lipids either in the adipose tissue or the oenocytes compared to control flies (Figure 3D, E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific co-expression of inrDN and pvrDN results in flies that are still obese with excessive lipid accumulation in adipose tissue but suppressed lipid accumulation in oenocytes.
claims.source: Strikingly, while oenots>pvrDN; inrDN flies were still obese and showed excessive accumulation of lipids in the adipose tissue, lipid accumulation in oenocytes was suppressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Right most panels, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating that InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation in the oenocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation in the oenocytes.
claims.source: Strikingly, while oenots>pvrDN; inrDN flies were still obese and showed excessive accumulation of lipids in the adipose tissue, lipid accumulation in oenocytes was suppressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Right most panels, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating that InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation in the oenocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential effects of InR and PvR signaling on oenocyte versus adipose tissue lipid accumulation.

claims.claim: A previous report showed that activation of InR signaling in oenocytes led to accumulation of lipids both under fed and starved conditions.
claims.source: Interestingly, a previous report showed that activation of InR signaling in oenocytes led to accumulation of lipids both under fed and starved conditions (Chatterjee et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Oenocyte-specific activation of TOR (by tsc2 knockdown) does not lead to lipid accumulation in oenocytes or adipose tissue.
claims.source: To further characterize the oenocyte-specific role of TOR on lipid accumulation, we activated TOR in the oenocytes (oenots>tsc2-i) and did not detect lipid accumulation either in the oenocytes or the adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

results.result: Muscle-specific knockdown of pvf1 in adult male Drosophila leads to an obesity phenotype characterized by increased lipid droplet size in adipose tissue, lipid accumulation in oenocytes, and significantly elevated whole-animal TAG content. This phenotype is specific to pvf1 (not pvf2 or pvf3), more pronounced on high-sugar diet, and results from metabolic defects rather than increased food intake.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are well-supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including BODIPY staining (Figures 1A-B), TAG assays with two independent RNAi lines (Figure 1C-D), dietary manipulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and radioactive glucose feeding assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). The tissue specificity, genetic specificity, and mechanistic distinction from feeding behavior are all experimentally demonstrated with appropriate controls.

results.result: Pvf1 protein is abundantly present in striated tubular leg muscles where it localizes between myofibrils and is concentrated at M and Z discs, but is absent from indirect flight muscles. Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown strongly reduces Pvf1 protein levels in leg muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 are supported by immunostaining data using anti-Pvf1 antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) showing both localization patterns in control flies and validation of knockdown efficiency. The tissue-specific distribution (tubular muscles vs IFMs) and subcellular localization are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Single-nuclei RNA-sequencing was performed on 80 adult fly abdominal cuticles in two biological replicates, yielding 15,280 nuclei with median 192 genes per nucleus after quality control with SoupX and batch correction with Harmony. Clustering at resolution 0.1 identified 10 unique clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C23 describe the snRNA-seq methodology and are well-documented with appropriate quality control metrics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D, Supplementary file 1). The use of established computational tools (SoupX, Harmony, Seurat) with proper citations and the reporting of key metrics (read depth, nuclei count, genes per nucleus) demonstrate methodological rigor.

results.result: Three major clusters from snRNA-seq were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers (apolpp, fasn3, mhc respectively). These assignments were validated using GAL4 lines showing that Pellino, sallimus, and geko specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31 are supported by both computational cluster analysis (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and experimental validation using tissue-specific GAL4 drivers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I). The combination of known marker genes and independent experimental validation provides strong support for cluster identity assignments.

results.result: Minor clusters (4-10) are inferred to represent remnant tissues including gut/malpighian tubule and ejaculatory bulb based on gene expression patterns. Higher resolution clustering (0.4) identifies 15 clusters that may reflect heterogeneity within adipose tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are based on inference from gene expression patterns without direct experimental validation of tissue identity. While the gene expression patterns are consistent with the proposed tissue identities (Supplementary file 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), the lack of independent validation and the speculative nature of the heterogeneity interpretation (C35) make these claims uncertain.

results.result: Pathway enrichment analysis reveals EGFR and PVR RTK signaling is highly enriched in oenocytes. Egfr is specifically enriched in adipose tissue while Pvr is highly enriched in oenocytes. Immunostaining confirms PvR is most prominent on oenocyte surfaces, followed by adipose tissue, and localizes to muscle sarcolemma with relatively weak levels in leg muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are well-supported by both computational pathway analysis (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3) and experimental validation through immunostaining (Figure 2D-E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). The concordance between snRNA-seq predictions and protein localization data strengthens these findings.

results.result: Oenocyte-specific loss of PvR signaling (via pvrDN overexpression or pvr RNAi) leads to obesity phenotypes similar to muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown, observed in both males and females. Over-expressing pvrDN in adipose tissue or muscle does not cause obesity, indicating Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 are strongly supported by tissue-specific genetic manipulations with appropriate controls (Figures 2F-G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-D). The tissue specificity is demonstrated through systematic testing across multiple tissues, and the sex-independence rules out confounding effects from male accessory glands. The inference that muscle-derived Pvf1 signals to oenocytes (C48) is well-supported by the combined data.

results.result: Two independent RNAi lines against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype of oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies, suggesting PvR regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism. Previous studies showed PvR can activate TOR pathway in cell culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by experimental data using two independent ERK RNAi lines (Figure 3A, C), providing genetic evidence against ERK involvement. The inference of ERK-independence (C50) is reasonable given the negative results with validated RNAi lines. C51 is appropriately cited to prior work.

results.result: Oenocyte-specific loss of TOR signaling (tsc1,tsc2 overexpression) or components of the Pi3K/Akt1 pathway (Pi3K92E, Pi3K21B, akt1 knockdown) leads to massive lipid accumulation in adipose tissue and oenocytes, indicating the Pi3K/Akt1/TOR pathway in oenocytes protects against obesity.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are well-supported by systematic genetic manipulation of pathway components with consistent phenotypic outcomes (Figures 3B-E). Multiple independent manipulations of the same pathway yielding similar phenotypes strengthens the conclusion. The inference that this pathway protects against obesity (C57) is justified by the data.

results.result: Both muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown and oenocyte-specific pvrDN expression show strong down-regulation of p4EBP (a TOR target) in oenocytes, similar to tsc1,tsc2 overexpression but unlike InR loss. This indicates muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in oenocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by quantitative immunostaining of p4EBP (Figures 4A-C) with appropriate positive (tsc1,tsc2) and negative (inrDN) controls. The use of a direct TOR target (p4EBP) as readout and the concordance across multiple genotypes support the inference that Pvf regulates TORC1 (C60).

results.result: Oenocyte-specific tsc2 knockdown strongly suppresses the obesity phenotype of pvrDN expression, and co-expression of constitutively active rheb completely rescues the phenotype, demonstrating TOR functions downstream of PvR in oenocytes to negatively regulate lipid deposits.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are strongly supported by genetic epistasis experiments (Figures 4D-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B). The rescue of the pvrDN phenotype by activating TOR signaling (either by tsc2 knockdown or rhebAV4 expression) provides compelling evidence for the pathway hierarchy. The inference of epistatic relationship (C65) is well-justified.

results.result: Oenocyte-specific InR loss does not increase lipid accumulation alone, but when combined with pvrDN, flies remain obese with adipose tissue lipid accumulation while oenocyte lipid accumulation is suppressed, indicating InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation specifically in oenocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by genetic interaction experiments (Figures 3D-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B). The differential tissue-specific effects of InR loss (suppressing oenocyte but not adipose tissue lipid accumulation in pvrDN background) provide strong evidence for the tissue-specific role of InR. C66 is established knowledge appropriately stated.

results.result: Previous work showed InR activation in oenocytes causes lipid accumulation. Oenocyte-specific TOR activation (tsc2 knockdown) does not cause lipid accumulation. Together, the data demonstrate muscle-derived Pvf1 signals through PvR in oenocytes to activate TOR, protecting against obesity.
results.evaluation: C70 is appropriately cited. C71 is supported by experimental data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D). C72 represents a well-justified synthesis of multiple experimental results showing the complete signaling pathway from muscle Pvf1 through oenocyte PvR to TOR activation and obesity protection.

results.result: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies show increased starvation resistance compared to controls, likely reflecting higher stored TAG levels that can be used for longer duration. Previous work established roles for oenocytes in starvation-induced lipid mobilization and VLCFA production.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 appropriately cite prior work. C76-C77 are supported by starvation resistance assays (Figure 5A). The inference about nutrient mobilization capability (C78) and the mechanistic explanation based on higher TAG stores (C79) are reasonable given the experimental data, though C79 remains somewhat speculative without direct measurement during starvation.

results.result: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown, oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 overexpression, and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies all show similar rates of lipid mobilization compared to controls, indicating loss of the muscle-to-oenocyte Pvf1 signaling axis does not impair lipid mobilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by radioisotope chase experiments measuring lipid mobilization rates (Figures 5B-C). The use of [1-14C]-oleate labeling followed by chase on cold food provides direct measurement of mobilization. The inference that the pathway does not affect mobilization (C83) is justified by the lack of differences across multiple genotypes.

results.result: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown, oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 overexpression, and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies all show increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions. In absence of effects on lipid mobilization, this indicates increased lipid synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by radioisotope incorporation experiments (Figures 5D-E). The inference that increased incorporation reflects increased synthesis (C87) is reasonable given the lack of mobilization defects, though alternative explanations (e.g., altered TAG turnover, changes in lipid trafficking) are not fully excluded.

results.result: In oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 overexpression flies, oenocyte-specific fatty acid synthases (fasn2, fasn3) are strongly downregulated while acc and fasn1 are unchanged. This indicates TOR loss downregulates oenocyte lipogenic genes, and the increased lipid synthesis occurs through a mechanism independent of TOR's role in regulating lipogenic gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 5F). The inferences (C90-C91) about the paradoxical increase in lipid synthesis despite reduced lipogenic gene expression are reasonable, though the mechanism remains unexplained. The authors appropriately acknowledge this paradox and suggest it requires further investigation.

results.result: Newly eclosed adult flies have low adipose tissue lipid content with small adipose cells. Over 3-7 days post-eclosion, adipose tissue builds up lipid stores through feeding and de novo synthesis, expanding significantly. Lipid droplet number per cell increases drastically with appearance of many smaller droplets, while average droplet size changes little, suggesting lipid buildup occurs through formation of new droplets that grow larger.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 are supported by time-course imaging data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with citation to prior work (C92). The detailed characterization of lipid droplet dynamics provides strong support. The inference about the mechanism of lipid buildup (C99) is reasonable based on the observed patterns, though direct tracking of individual droplets over time would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Muscle-specific pvf1 expression is low in newly eclosed flies and increases rapidly over 7 days. Premature muscle-specific pvf1 overexpression from day 1 leads to fewer large lipid droplets per adipose cell and more empty adipose cells, suggesting muscle-derived Pvf1 helps terminate the adipose tissue lipid buildup phase by suppressing lipid synthesis via oenocyte signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by RT-qPCR showing temporal expression (Figure 6A) and imaging/quantification of lipid droplets in overexpression flies (Figures 6B-D). The inference about Pvf1's role in terminating lipid buildup (C103) is well-supported by the temporal correlation and functional effects of premature expression.

results.result: Muscle-Pvf1 serves as an inhibitory signal for suppressing de novo lipid synthesis once adult adipose tissue has accumulated sufficient lipid stores at the end of the lipid build-up phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C140 (identical) represent the main conclusion integrating temporal expression data, gain-of-function experiments, and mechanistic studies. This synthesis is well-supported by the collective evidence showing: (1) pvf1 expression increases as lipid buildup completes, (2) premature expression inhibits buildup, (3) loss of function increases lipid synthesis, and (4) the pathway acts through oenocytes.

results.result: The snRNA-seq dataset of adult abdominal region will serve as a resource for understanding adipose tissue, oenocyte, and muscle biology. A searchable webtool was created for data exploration.
results.evaluation: C105 is speculative about future utility but reasonable given the comprehensive nature of the dataset. C106 is factually supported by the description of the created resource with provided URL. The data deposition in GEO (GSE147601) enables reproducibility.

results.result: PDGF/VEGF ligands co-evolved with multicellularity and signal in organisms with tissue-level organization. In vertebrates, VEGF-A/B and PDGF-BB/-CC influence metabolic responses including adiposity and insulin resistance, though mechanisms are complex and context-dependent. Previous studies attributed effects to vascularization, but signaling to non-endothelial cells could be equally important.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C112 appropriately cite and summarize prior literature. C113 is speculation but reasonable given the context. These claims provide appropriate background and motivation for the study.

results.result: In Drosophila, PDGF/VEGF pathway ligands are encoded by pvf1, pvf2, and pvf3, which signal through the RTK Pvr to activate Ras/Raf/ERK. Pvf1 is closely related to both VEGFs and PDGFs. Pvf2 and Pvf3 are more ancestral and phylogenetically distinct, with Pvf2 lacking the conserved cysteine for cysteine knot formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119 appropriately cite established knowledge about Drosophila PDGF/VEGF signaling and phylogenetic relationships. These provide necessary background for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: Core metabolic organs and signaling mechanisms are highly conserved between Drosophila and vertebrates. Drosophila adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscles are functionally analogous to vertebrate adipose tissue, liver, and skeletal muscle. Various hormonal signals and the TOR pathway are conserved and well-studied in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C129 appropriately cite established knowledge about Drosophila as a metabolic model system. These provide essential context for the significance of the findings and justify the use of Drosophila for studying metabolic regulation.

results.result: Drosophila Pvfs have been primarily studied in development and immunity, with metabolic roles less explored. This study identifies Pvf1 as a muscle-derived myokine regulating systemic lipid stores by inhibiting lipid synthesis, with oenocytes as primary targets identified by snRNA-seq. Pvf1 signals through PvR/Pi3K/Akt1/TOR in oenocytes and regulates adipose tissue lipid buildup in newly eclosed flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 appropriately summarize prior work and knowledge gaps. C132-C135 represent the main findings of the study and are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript, integrating genetic, molecular, and metabolic data.

results.result: Flies eclose with limited adipose tissue lipid stores and enter a developmental stage marked by increased lipid synthesis for lipid store accumulation. Muscle pvf1 expression increases rapidly during this stage, and premature expression interferes with lipid accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 are supported by imaging data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), RT-qPCR (Figure 6A), and gain-of-function experiments (Figures 6B-D). The temporal correlation between pvf1 expression and lipid buildup completion, combined with functional interference by premature expression, provides strong support.

results.result: This is the first evidence in a metazoan of a PDGF/VEGF ligand acting as a myokine that regulates systemic lipid homeostasis by activating TOR in hepatocyte-like cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 represents the novelty statement of the study. Based on the cited literature and the comprehensive experimental evidence presented, this claim of novelty appears justified. The study demonstrates a non-endothelial, metabolic role for PDGF/VEGF signaling through TOR activation in hepatocyte-like cells, which has not been previously reported in metazoans.
